Prediction Intervals: Bootstrap and GAM-Bayes Methods

Source: vignettes/prediction-intervals.Rmd
prediction-intervals.Rmd

Overview

Point forecasts alone are insufficient for mortality planning — actuaries, public health officials, and pension funds need uncertainty quantification. mortensor provides two complementary approaches to prediction intervals (PIs):

  1. Residual bootstrap: Resamples historical residuals and simulates future time-series paths (fast, model-agnostic)
  2. GAM-Bayes posterior propagation: Draws from the GAM smoothing posterior, re-runs the forecast pipeline on each draw, capturing both smoothing uncertainty and model uncertainty (slower, more thorough)

Both methods produce 95% prediction intervals and optionally store the full simulation array for custom quantile extraction.

The add_pi() function

add_pi() is the main entry point. It takes a mort_forecast object (from forecast()) and augments it with PI bounds:

library(mortensor)
data(example_mortality)

sm  <- smooth_mortality(example_mortality, method = "gam",
                        covid_years = c(2020L, 2021L))
cal <- calibrate(sm, holdout_frac = 0.2, ensemble = TRUE)
fc  <- forecast(cal, h = 10)

# Add prediction intervals
fc <- add_pi(fc, n_sim = 500, method = "bootstrap")

Parameters 

fc <- add_pi(
  fc,
  n_sim       = 500L,          # number of bootstrap/posterior draws
  method      = "bootstrap",   # "bootstrap" or "gam_bayes"
  cap         = 1.5,           # cap extreme simulations at cap × point forecast
  calibration = NULL           # mort_calibration (needed for gam_bayes)
)

After add_pi(), the forecast object gains:

  • fc$mx_lower: 3D array of 2.5th percentile (lower 95% bound)
  • fc$mx_upper: 3D array of 97.5th percentile (upper 95% bound)
  • fc$mx_median: 3D array of median forecast
  • fc$sims: 4D array [n_ages × h × n_groups × n_sim] (full simulations)

Method 1: Residual bootstrap

How it works

The bootstrap method resamples historical forecast residuals and adds them to simulated future paths:

  1. Compute residuals: ex,t,g=log(m̂x,t,g)−log(mx,t,g)e_{x,t,g} = \log(\hat{m}_{x,t,g}) - \log(m_{x,t,g}) where m̂\hat{m} are in-sample fitted values.
  2. Resample residuals: Draw BB bootstrap samples of the residual array (sampling years with replacement, preserving cross-sectional dependence within each year).
  3. Simulate time-series paths: For Tucker3, re-simulate the ARIMA/ETS fits on the B-mode using forecast::simulate(). For Lee-Carter/FDM, simulate the kt (period index) process.
  4. Reconstruct: Combine resampled residuals with simulated paths to produce BB forecast surfaces.
  5. Extract quantiles: The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles across simulations give the 95% PI.

Tucker3 bootstrap 

# The forecast must have been produced with return_full = TRUE
# (this happens automatically when using the calibrate → forecast workflow)

fc_boot <- add_pi(fc, n_sim = 500, method = "bootstrap")

# Inspect dimensions
dim(fc_boot$sims)       # [13, 10, 10, 500] for 13 ages, 10 years, 10 groups
dim(fc_boot$mx_lower)   # [13, 10, 10]
dim(fc_boot$mx_upper)   # [13, 10, 10]

Lee-Carter / FDM bootstrap

For demography-based models, bootstrap_lc_fdm() uses the demography package’s built-in simulation:

# When the best model is Lee-Carter, add_pi() dispatches automatically
cal_lc <- calibrate(sm, models = "lee_carter", ensemble = FALSE)
fc_lc  <- forecast(cal_lc, h = 10)
fc_lc  <- add_pi(fc_lc, n_sim = 500, method = "bootstrap")

StMoMo bootstrap

For StMoMo models, bootstrap_stmomo() uses the package’s semi-parametric bootstrap:

# Requires StMoMo package
cal_sm <- calibrate(sm, models = "stmomo", ensemble = FALSE)
fc_sm  <- forecast(cal_sm, h = 10)
fc_sm  <- add_pi(fc_sm, n_sim = 500, method = "bootstrap")

Ensemble bootstrap

When the forecast is from an ensemble, each member produces its own simulation array. These are combined using the ensemble weights:

# With an ensemble calibration, add_pi() handles the combination
cal_ens <- calibrate(sm, ensemble = TRUE, ensemble_top_k = 3)
fc_ens  <- forecast(cal_ens, h = 10)
fc_ens  <- add_pi(fc_ens, n_sim = 500, method = "bootstrap")

# The weights from calibration are used to blend simulations
cat("Ensemble members:", fc_ens$extras$ensemble_names, "\n")

Internally, ensemble_bootstrap() draws from each model’s simulation array with probability equal to the ensemble weight, producing a blended set of simulations.

Method 2: GAM-Bayes posterior propagation

How it works

The GAM-Bayes method propagates uncertainty from the smoothing stage through the entire pipeline:

  1. Draw from GAM posterior: The 2D P-spline GAM (from smooth_mortality()) has a posterior distribution over its coefficients. Using mgcv::rmvn() (multivariate normal), draw BB coefficient vectors from 𝛃̂∼𝒩(𝛃̂,𝐕β)\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sim \mathcal{N}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}, \mathbf{V}_{\beta}).
  2. Reconstruct smoothed surfaces: For each draw, predict new smoothed mortality arrays.
  3. Re-run the forecast: For each smoothed draw, run the full ensemble forecast pipeline (using the same calibrated ranks/models).
  4. Collect simulations: This yields BB forecast surfaces that reflect both smoothing uncertainty and forecast uncertainty.

Usage 

# GAM-Bayes requires the calibration object (for model parameters)
fc_gb <- add_pi(fc, n_sim = 200, method = "gam_bayes",
                calibration = cal)

# This is slower (re-runs forecast for each posterior draw)
# but captures a broader uncertainty envelope

When to use GAM-Bayes

Criterion Bootstrap GAM-Bayes
Speed Fast (seconds) Slow (minutes)
Uncertainty sources Forecast model only Smoothing + forecast
Width of PIs Narrower Wider (more honest)
Small samples May underestimate Better calibrated
Ensemble Per-model bootstrap Full pipeline re-run

For publication-quality results, GAM-Bayes is recommended with n_sim >= 500. For exploratory analysis, bootstrap with n_sim = 200 is often sufficient.

Custom quantile extraction

The full simulation array allows extracting arbitrary quantiles:

# 80% prediction interval
pi80_lower <- apply(fc$sims, c(1, 2, 3), quantile, probs = 0.10)
pi80_upper <- apply(fc$sims, c(1, 2, 3), quantile, probs = 0.90)

# 50% prediction interval (interquartile range)
pi50_lower <- apply(fc$sims, c(1, 2, 3), quantile, probs = 0.25)
pi50_upper <- apply(fc$sims, c(1, 2, 3), quantile, probs = 0.75)

# Probability of mortality exceeding a threshold
threshold <- 0.01  # 1% mortality rate
prob_exceed <- apply(fc$sims, c(1, 2, 3), function(x) mean(x > threshold))

Visualising prediction intervals

Fan charts 

# PI fan chart for a specific group
plot(fc, type = "pi")

# Trend plot with PI envelope
plot(fc, type = "trends")

By-age trend fans 

# Fan charts faceted by age group
plot(fc, type = "trends")  # age-averaged with PI ribbon

Smoothing uncertainty (GAM-Bayes)

When using GAM-Bayes, you can also visualise the smoothing credible intervals:

# Compute GAM credible intervals on the smoothed surface
ci <- compute_gam_ci_arrays(sm$gam_fits, sm$ages, sm$years)
# ci$mx_lo, ci$mx_hi: 3D arrays of 95% credible bounds

# These feed into the GAM-Bayes procedure

Capping extreme simulations

Bootstrap simulations can occasionally produce extreme values, especially at older ages or long horizons. The cap parameter in add_pi() truncates simulations:

m̃x,t,g(b)=min(mx,t,g(b),cap×m̂x,t,g) \tilde{m}^{(b)}_{x,t,g} = \min\bigl(m^{(b)}_{x,t,g},\;\text{cap} \times \hat{m}_{x,t,g}\bigr)

The default cap = 1.5 limits any simulation to 150% of the point forecast.

# More permissive cap for long horizons
fc_wide <- add_pi(fc, n_sim = 500, method = "bootstrap", cap = 2.0)

# Stricter cap for short horizons
fc_tight <- add_pi(fc, n_sim = 500, method = "bootstrap", cap = 1.2)

Prediction intervals for life expectancy

Once PIs are attached to the forecast, life_expectancy() propagates them:

le <- life_expectancy(fc)
head(le)
#    year      group     ex  ex_lower  ex_upper
# 1: 2021   Male_Q1  47.12     45.89     48.31
# 2: 2021   Male_Q2  48.56     47.21     49.87
# ...

# The PI on life expectancy is derived from the simulation array:
# for each simulation, compute life_table() → ex, then take quantiles

Prediction intervals for disaggregated data

After disaggregation, PIs are transferred to single-year ages using ratio scaling:

fc_pi <- add_pi(fc, n_sim = 500, method = "bootstrap")
fc_1yr <- disaggregate(fc_pi, target_ages = 30:100,
                       method = "natural_gompertz")

# The extras contain disaggregated PIs
head(fc_1yr$extras$mx_1yr_dt)
#    year age      group   mx_point  mx_lo95  mx_hi95  mx_median
# 1: 2021  30   Male_Q1   0.00052   0.00041  0.00064   0.00051

Complete example 

library(mortensor)
data(example_mortality)

# Pipeline
sm  <- smooth_mortality(example_mortality, method = "gam",
                        covid_years = c(2020L, 2021L))
cal <- calibrate(sm, holdout_frac = 0.2, ensemble = TRUE)
fc  <- forecast(cal, h = 10)

# Bootstrap PIs (fast)
fc_boot <- add_pi(fc, n_sim = 500, method = "bootstrap")
plot(fc_boot, type = "pi")
plot(fc_boot, type = "trends")

# GAM-Bayes PIs (thorough)
fc_bayes <- add_pi(fc, n_sim = 200, method = "gam_bayes",
                   calibration = cal)
plot(fc_bayes, type = "pi")

# Compare PI widths
boot_width  <- mean(log(fc_boot$mx_upper)  - log(fc_boot$mx_lower))
bayes_width <- mean(log(fc_bayes$mx_upper) - log(fc_bayes$mx_lower))
cat(sprintf("Average PI width (log scale): bootstrap=%.3f, gam_bayes=%.3f\n",
            boot_width, bayes_width))

# Life expectancy with PIs
le <- life_expectancy(fc_boot)
print(le)

# Export everything
export(fc_boot, dir = "results/")

Summary

Feature bootstrap gam_bayes
Uncertainty source Model residuals + TS simulation GAM posterior + full re-forecast
Speed (500 sims) ~10 seconds ~5 minutes
PI calibration Good for large samples Better for small samples
Ensemble support Per-model, then blend Full pipeline per draw
Custom quantiles Via sims array Via sims array

Both methods attach to the mort_forecast object seamlessly, so downstream operations (disaggregate(), life_expectancy(), export(), plot()) work identically regardless of which method was used.
